rv.q: This is one hell of a ride, and not just because of the gore — though there's plenty of that.

"The challenge is to get someone who knows the story anxious all over again. And that they do. The box-office catnip is Willis, totally convincing in his first play since his early off-Broadway days…But the wow factor, the precision instrument that keeps propelling the story into psychologically unexpected corners, is Laurie Metcalf...
It’s a stunning performance, even if, in this oddly fear-free production, she provokes more pity than terror.
Nowhere this season on Broadway is there an acting gulf as wide between two leads than here.
Willis's weirdly narcotized and passive Broadway debut goes above and beyond the drugged, physically diminished circumstances of his character.
But despite a story that’s serviceably creepy and a handsome production starring Bruce Willis and Laurie Metcalf, what this production mostly demonstrates is the futility of digging up the dead.

The production that opened on Sunday night at the Broadhurst Theater, which stars a vacant Bruce Willis (in his Broadway debut) and a hardworking Laurie Metcalf, sustains a steady, drowsy room temperature throughout.

But the lack of a zesty scene partner who is really going to challenge her and go for broke eventually seems to wear Metcalf down — it is like watching a two-hander with one of the hands shrouded in mist.
Willis, though well-cast (taciturn suffering has more or less become his thing), just doesn’t seem particularly endangered.
Nor is there any other reason to go to “Misery,” which has nothing else to offer save for the chance to get Mr. Willis’s autograph after the show.
'Misery' is a scream. I was never bored and didn't want it to end.
Just one of the many pleasures of this tremendously entertaining show is getting to figure out what makes her tick (and hobble).
However, what they'll find at the Broadhurst theater is more comic than chilling and suspenseful.
However, though the technical specs are excellent, the production suffers from a curious lack of tension.

Those with a limited tolerance for such mockery - and sometimes gruesome antics (fans looking forward to a scene involving Paul’s ankles won’t be disappointed) -- may feel uncomfortable watching the fun this Misery has at the expense of both main characters.
Die-HARD? Die-easy is more like it.
Despite Metcalf's excellently maniacal Annie, the tension here is more discomfort than terror
Unfortunately, it’s not just Paul’s legs that are hobbled here, it’s the entire show.
Frankly, this “Misery” doesn’t have enough over-the-top physical torture and mayhem to relieve its long spells of tedium.
It's not a bad time, but when you're a millisecond away from witnessing a brutal act and you and the people around you can barely stifle snickers, it's not exactly a good time, either.
It's a cat-and-mouse game in which only the cat is committed to playing.
Those who don’t see the humor are likely to find it a pointless star vehicle.

Misery is harmless — and really, what's the point of that?
Except for an instant when Willis brashly flashes his nemesis the bird, he's so bland it's frightening.
What might seem creepy on film plays as silly and campy on stage.
There are not enough superlatives to describe her singular performance.
What makes it all work however, is the contrasting and beautiful work of both stars.
MISERY on Broadway is a bit of tasty popcorn elevated to high art by an exceptional stage actor.
Misery certainly is not miserable and it deserves to be seen.

“Misery” won’t necessarily make you sad, or happy, but it does the job of thrilling and chilling quite well – in addition to providing yet another showcase for the titanic talent known as Laurie Metcalf.
It’s a stunning performance, even if, in this oddly fear-free production, she provokes more pity than terror.
The work is truly terrifying at moments but fails to keep the intensity throughout.
Misery, the play, will be remembered for Bruce Willis’ mild Broadway debut and Laurie Metcalf’s bravura performance.
I actually ended up not minding the show at all.
Willis, on the other hand, is strangely one-dimensional, as though trying with all effort not to let any part of his "Die Hard" or other super-hero film characters be seen.
As a play, “Misery” just seems ridiculous, over the top, and in the end, pointless.
A play like this is a kind of game; here, however, only one person on stage is playing for keeps.
Although it’s not a great acting vehicle for Willis, it does at least share that trait with his films.
We know Mr. Willis is a great superhero on the screen; unfortunately, he is one-dimensional on the stage.
The other sad element that drags this production so far down that it barely has a pulse is the performance of Mr. Willis.
Although he does manage some priceless blank stares, his acting registers as something close to a non-performance in a 1,100-seat Broadway house.

Attempting to pull the wool over the eyes of some theater patrons who should know better than to be fooled by star casting, playing it for laughs, gimmicks and a cheesy script that has more holes than there are in a huge chunk of Swiss.
